highlights.quote: Absorbed dose \(D\) is the radiation energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue.

highlights.quote: Absorbed dose \(D\) is the radiation energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue.
It increases with the strength of the source, the time of exposure and closeness to the source.
Equivalent dose \(H\) weights that absorbed dose for the radiation type: α causes denser ionization than β, γ or X-rays.

Effective dose \(E\) then weights the equivalent dose for the sensitivity of the exposed tissue, so it can represent the overall risk from an exposure: \[ H = D \times W_{\text{radiation}}, \qquad E = H \times W_{\text{tissue}} \] For exposure involving several tissues, add the appropriately weighted contributions to obtain \(E\).
Equivalent and effective dose are measured in sievert (Sv); one sievert is large, so everyday values are quoted in millisieverts (mSv).

highlights.quote: Absorbed dose \(D\) is the radiation energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue.
It increases with the strength of the source, the time of exposure and closeness to the source.
Equivalent dose \(H\) weights that absorbed dose for the radiation type: α causes denser ionization than β, γ or X-rays.

Effective dose \(E\) then weights the equivalent dose for the sensitivity of the exposed tissue, so it can represent the overall risk from an exposure: \[ H = D \times W_{\text{radiation}}, \qquad E = H \times W_{\text{tissue}} \] For exposure involving several tissues, add the appropriately weighted contributions to obtain \(E\).
Equivalent and effective dose are measured in sievert (Sv); one sievert is large, so everyday values are quoted in millisieverts (mSv).

highlights.quote: α, β, γ and X-rays carry enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms.
In living tissue this breaks up molecules in cells, in particular DNA.
A cell may die, or its damaged DNA may make it divide uncontrollably, which is cancer.
Damage to reproductive cells can be passed to offspring.
The effects are cumulative: many small doses add up.

highlights.quote: Dry ice cools the base of the chamber.

highlights.quote: An unstable nuclide (a radionuclide or radioisotope) gets rid of excess energy by emitting radiation; this is radioactive decay.
The original nucleus is the parent, the nucleus left behind is the daughter.
When the daughter is a different element (different \( Z \)) the change is a transmutation.
Decay is spontaneous and random: nothing outside the nucleus (heat, pressure, chemical bonding) starts, stops, speeds or slows it.

highlights.quote: Because only α changes \( A \), and by 4 each time, every member of a series has a mass number that differs from the parent's by a multiple of 4.

highlights.quote: The decay constant \( k \) of a nuclide is the instantaneous probability per unit time that one undecayed nucleus decays; equivalently, it is the instantaneous fraction of undecayed nuclei that decay per unit time.
Unit: s-1 (or min-1, h-1, y-1).
For a very short interval \( \Delta t \), the probability is approximately \( k\Delta t \).
Over a whole second, if \( k = 0.2 \) s-1, the exact probability is \( 1-e^{-0.2}=0.181 \), not exactly \( 0.2 \).

When the daughter is a different element (different \( Z \)) the change is a transmutation.
Decay is spontaneous and random: nothing outside the nucleus (heat, pressure, chemical bonding) starts, stops, speeds or slows it.

highlights.quote: The decay constant \( k \) of a nuclide is the instantaneous probability per unit time that one undecayed nucleus decays; equivalently, it is the instantaneous fraction of undecayed nuclei that decay per unit time.
Unit: s-1 (or min-1, h-1, y-1).
For a very short interval \( \Delta t \), the probability is approximately \( k\Delta t \).
Over a whole second, if \( k = 0.2 \) s-1, the exact probability is \( 1-e^{-0.2}=0.181 \), not exactly \( 0.2 \).

highlights.quote: Natural carbon is about 99% carbon-12 and 1% carbon-13, both stable, with a trace (about one atom in \( 10^{12} \)) of radioactive carbon-14.

C-14 is made continuously in the upper atmosphere when cosmic-ray neutrons strike nitrogen, \( {}^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} \rightarrow {}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C} + {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{p} \), and it decays by β emission, \( {}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C} \rightarrow {}^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{0}_{-1}e \).
Production balances decay, so the C-14 fraction in atmospheric carbon dioxide stays roughly constant.

Mass can be converted into energy according to \[ E = \Delta m\, c^{2} \] where \(E\) is the energy released, \(\Delta m\) is the mass defect (loss in mass) and \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) is the speed of light in vacuum.

highlights.quote: α, β, γ and X-rays carry enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms.
In living tissue this breaks up molecules in cells, in particular DNA.
A cell may die, or its damaged DNA may make it divide uncontrollably, which is cancer.
Damage to reproductive cells can be passed to offspring.
The effects are cumulative: many small doses add up.
